evidence.note: Explicit ordered milestones: probe env, write correct reference kernel (step 5), build test_correct.py as an independent correctness oracle/done-check (step 6), only then build bench.py to measure baseline latency across the 10 timed shapes (step 7). Clear correctness-before-speed staging.

Optimization stage is decomposed per-component (LN, proj5, bmm, fused_final) with repeated profile*.py breakdowns and per-shape tuning; each optimization change is followed by re-running test_correct/profile as an exit check, so regressions are localized to the component just touched.

Per-milestone fast-but-wrong prevention: bf16 casts that sped things up but broke Cauchy correctness (max_abs > 2e-2) were detected and reverted, keeping the correct baseline frozen — exactly the guard the high anchors describe.

At the end, correctness across normal/cauchy/mask is treated as the satisfied gate while latency (11.8ms vs 10.4ms) is a separate, still-open objective; agent submits on correctness priority. Shows the two milestones were kept distinct through the whole horizon.

reasoning: The agent's process matches the level-8 anchor precisely: milestones are ordered (reference oracle → correct baseline verified across shapes/distributions/mask → latency tuning against the 10 timed shapes), each with a concrete exit test, and regressions stay localized because correctness is re-checked after each component change. It reaches into level-10 territory by decomposing the optimization stage per-component and per-shape with per-milestone checks that caught and reverted fast-but-wrong bf16 changes, but falls short of a full 10 because risk-sequencing (nailing the hardest Cauchy/large-N numerics first as a deliberate first milestone) was reactive rather than front-loaded and performance was not run as a formally separate track on a frozen baseline.
